title: Give Home Assistant a home: Raspberry Pi
summary: Install Home Assistant OS on a Raspberry Pi, protect the card's old files, and open Home Assistant in a browser.
outcomes: Explain host, operating system and Home Assistant OS in plain words
List the Pi, power supply, card, card reader and Ethernet cable you need
Write the image to the right card, open Home Assistant and record the result

slides.title: One computer keeps the system running
body: Host = the computer that runs Home Assistant
Home Assistant OS = an operating system built for it
slides.narration: Lesson C one named the host: the computer that runs Home Assistant, the software that collects readings and switches equipment. This lesson builds the host on a Raspberry Pi, the credit-card-sized computer. Lesson C two B builds it on a PC instead, and you need only one. Every computer needs an operating system: the base software that starts it and runs its programs, as Windows does on a laptop. You will install Home Assistant OS, an operating system made only to run Home Assistant. Look at the picture on screen. Readings come in, messages go out, and one always-on host sits in the middle. If you already have a working Home Assistant host, check it and skip ahead to lesson C three. Keep pumps and valves disconnected while you set up.

visual.title: One computer keeps the system running
visual.alt: Choose one supported always-on computer: Raspberry Pi OR a dedicated x86-64 host.

check.prompt: You already run a working Home Assistant host. What do you do next?

options.text: Check it, then go to lesson C3
options.feedback: Right. One host is enough. Check its version and backups in C3 rather than starting again.

options.text: Install Home Assistant again on a new Pi
options.feedback: A second host adds nothing. Keep the working one and continue to C3.

options.text: Complete both C2a and C2b
options.feedback: C2a and C2b are alternatives. You need one host, and you already have it.

slides.title: Lay out the parts first
body: Pi 4 or Pi 5 · 2 GB memory or more · its own power supply
microSD card 32 GB+ (A2) · card reader · Ethernet cable
slides.narration: Before you start, lay the parts out on a table, as the screen shows. You need a Raspberry Pi four or Pi five with at least two gigabytes of memory, the working space it uses while running. You need a storage card: a micro S D card, the small memory card used in cameras and phones, of at least thirty-two gigabytes. The official guide suggests one marked A two, a speed rating printed on the card. You need a card reader for your everyday computer. You need the power supply made for that Pi model, because phone chargers and computer USB ports often cannot supply enough power. Last, you need an Ethernet cable: the network cable with a clip-on plug that joins the Pi to your router. The official guide requires it for installation. Check the current official guide before you buy, because its list can change.

visual.title: Lay out the parts first

check.prompt: Which power source should run the Pi?

options.text: The power supply made for that Pi model
options.feedback: Right. It delivers enough steady power. A weak supply can make the Pi restart at random.

options.text: A spare USB port on your laptop
options.feedback: Computer USB ports do not supply enough power for a Pi running Home Assistant.

options.text: Any phone charger with the same plug
options.feedback: A plug that fits can still supply too little power. Use the supply made for the Pi.

slides.title: Example: choose the spare card
body: Image = one file that is a copy of a ready card
Write to the checked 64 GB card; leave the 1 TB drive
slides.narration: Writing the software is different from copying a file. Home Assistant OS comes as an image: one file that is an exact copy of a ready-to-run storage card. Writing the image copies it onto your card and replaces everything already on it. The tool for this is Raspberry Pi Imager, a free program from the makers of the Pi that runs on your everyday computer. Now imagine Imager lists two places to write: a spare sixty-four gigabyte card and a one terabyte photo drive. Look at the two choices on screen. You choose the sixty-four gigabyte card, because it is the spare you checked and backed up. You leave the photo drive alone. In Imager, choose OS, then Other specific-purpose OS, then Home assistants and home automation, then Home Assistant. Pick the build for your Pi four or Pi five, then choose the checked card as storage.

visual.title: Example: choose the spare card

workedExample.prompt: Imager lists a spare 64 GB card and a 1 TB photo drive. Which is ready to receive the image?
steps: Identify the spare 64 GB card by its name and capacity.
Check any files you need from it are copied elsewhere.
Choose the Home Assistant OS build for your exact Pi model.
workedExample.answer: Only the identified, backed-up 64 GB card. Writing replaces everything on it.

check.prompt: Imager lists a 32 GB card holding your only copy of family photos. Can you write to it?

options.text: Not yet. Copy the photos somewhere else first
options.feedback: Right. Writing replaces everything on the card. Save what you need before you write.

options.text: Yes. Imager keeps the old files
options.feedback: Writing an image replaces all the card's contents. The photos would be gone.

options.text: Yes. Only the photo drive gets erased
options.feedback: Only the storage you select is replaced, and here that is the card holding the photos.

slides.title: Your turn: the last check before Write
body: Say which card will be erased and where backups are
Next → Write → Finish; then card, Ethernet, power last
slides.narration: Pause before you press Write. Say this sentence out loud: I am replacing everything on this card, and any files I need are saved somewhere else. Add the Pi model and the matching image you chose. If any part is uncertain, sort it out first. Then select Next, then Write, and wait until Imager says the write has finished. Select Finish, then eject the card, meaning tell your computer it is safe to remove. The screen shows the next three steps in order. Push the card into the Pi while the Pi has no power. Plug the Ethernet cable from the Pi into the same router as your everyday computer. Connect the power supply last.

visual.title: Your turn: the last check before Write
labels: Name the card to be erased

check.prompt: In which order do you connect the Pi?

options.text: Card, then Ethernet, then power
options.feedback: Right. The Pi starts as soon as it has power, so the card and network go in first.

options.text: Power, then the card
options.feedback: The Pi starts on power. Insert the card while it is unpowered.

options.text: Power, then Ethernet, then the card
options.feedback: Power goes last. With no card in, the Pi has nothing to start from.

slides.title: Open Home Assistant in a browser
body: Open http://homeassistant.local in a web browser
If it fails, add :8123, the Home Assistant port
slides.narration: Your everyday computer now needs to find the Pi. Every device on your network has a network address, like a house number on a street. Your web browser uses it to reach that device. Wait a few minutes after power-on. Then type homeassistant dot local into the browser, as the screen shows. If nothing opens, add colon eight one two three to the end. That number is a port: a numbered door on the host where Home Assistant answers. You can also use the Pi's numbered network address, listed in your router's settings, followed by colon eight one two three. When the page opens, check it belongs to this new Pi and not an older system. You will then see onboarding: the short set of welcome screens Home Assistant shows on its first start. Lesson C three walks through them. A working page shows the host is reachable; the probes and water get their own checks later.

visual.title: Open Home Assistant in a browser

check.prompt: homeassistant.local does not open after a few minutes. What do you try next?

options.text: homeassistant.local:8123
options.feedback: Right. Adding the port number sends the browser to the door where Home Assistant answers.

options.text: Write the card again straight away
options.feedback: Try the port address first. The official guide suggests rewriting only if nothing appears after five minutes.

options.text: Connect the pump to see if it responds
options.feedback: Pumps stay disconnected during setup. Finding the page is a network question.

slides.title: Keep a way back
body: Record Pi model, card, version and working address
No page after 5 minutes: check power, cable, guide
slides.narration: Now try a different case. A card holds old research files with no other copy. Before writing, you copy those files somewhere safe and identify the card again. For your real installation, keep a written record, as the screen shows. Note the Pi model, the card size, the Home Assistant version and the address that worked. If no page appears after five minutes, check the power supply and the network cable. Then follow the official troubleshooting steps, which may mean writing the card again, perhaps on a different card. With this record, another person could rebuild your host. Lesson C three picks up at onboarding, then adds the Crop Steering software, accounts and backups.

visual.title: Keep a way back

check.prompt: Which record lets someone rebuild your host later?

options.text: Pi model, card, version and the address that worked
options.feedback: Right. Those details let another person repeat the setup and find the host.

options.text: A photo of the Pi on the shelf
options.feedback: A photo shows where it sits, not how it was built or reached.

options.text: Only the account password
options.feedback: A password lets you in, but rebuilding needs the model, card, version and address.

quiz.prompt: What happens to the chosen card when you write the image?

options.text: Its existing contents are replaced
options.feedback: Right. Save any files you need and check the card's name and size before writing.

options.text: Home Assistant is added beside the existing files
options.feedback: Writing an image replaces the whole card. Nothing old stays beside it.

options.text: Every connected disk is erased
options.feedback: Only the storage you select is replaced, which is why you check the selection carefully.

quiz.prompt: Which power supply is ready for the Pi?

options.text: One made for that exact Pi model
options.feedback: Right. It supplies enough steady power for the Pi to run reliably.

options.text: Any charger with the same plug
options.feedback: A matching plug can still supply too little power. Check it is made for your Pi.

options.text: A computer USB port
options.feedback: Computer USB ports do not supply enough power for a Pi running Home Assistant.

quiz.prompt: A suitable PC already runs Home Assistant well. What next?

options.text: Check it and continue to lesson C3
options.feedback: Right. The Pi and PC routes are alternatives, and one host is enough.

options.text: Buy a Pi because both hosts are required
options.feedback: Only one host is needed. Both routes reach the same place.

options.text: Erase the PC to match this lesson
options.feedback: Erasing a working host loses your setup. Keep it and continue to C3.

quiz.prompt: The new Pi opens its Home Assistant page. What have you shown?

options.text: The host is reachable; probes and water are checked later
options.feedback: Right. The page proves the network path. Equipment gets its own checks in later lessons.

options.text: The correct valve delivers water
options.feedback: No equipment is connected yet. Water is tested during supervised checks later.

options.text: Every dripper has its measured flow
options.feedback: Flow comes from a catch test with cups and a stopwatch, not from a web page.

title: Give Home Assistant a home: dedicated PC
summary: Install Home Assistant OS on a dedicated x86-64 PC, using a live Ubuntu USB stick, after checking the disk and protecting its files.
outcomes: Explain x86-64 PC, UEFI, Secure Boot and logical sectors in plain words
Tell the temporary live Ubuntu USB stick apart from the destination disk
Restore the image to the right disk, open Home Assistant and record the result

slides.title: Another home for Home Assistant
body: x86-64 PC = a computer with an Intel or AMD processor
Dedicated: it does this one job. Pi OR PC, not both
slides.narration: Lesson C one named the host: the computer that runs Home Assistant, the software that collects readings and switches equipment. This lesson builds the host on an x eighty-six sixty-four PC. That is a computer with an Intel or AMD processor, the chip design most desktop computers use. Lesson C two A uses a Raspberry Pi instead, and you need only one. A popular choice is a NUC, a palm-sized box PC. Its small shape alone does not make it suitable, so the next slide checks the details. The PC must be dedicated, meaning it does this one job and nothing else. The card shows that one host is enough. If you already have a working Home Assistant host, check it and skip ahead to lesson C three. Keep pumps and valves disconnected while you set up.

visual.title: Another home for Home Assistant
visual.alt: Pi and x86-64 are alternative host routes; only one host is needed.

check.prompt: Your Raspberry Pi already runs Home Assistant well. Do you also need this PC?

options.text: No. One host is enough
options.feedback: Right. The Pi and PC routes are alternatives that reach the same place.

options.text: Yes. The PC runs the Controller
options.feedback: Both Crop Steering parts run on the one host. A second computer is not needed.

options.text: Yes. The Pi only handles readings
options.feedback: One host does every job: readings, settings and watering decisions.

slides.title: Check the computer before changing it
body: 64-bit processor · starts with UEFI · Secure Boot off
Disk with 512-byte logical sectors; back up first
slides.narration: Every computer needs an operating system: the base software that starts it and runs its programs, as Windows does on a laptop. You will install Home Assistant OS, an operating system made only to run Home Assistant. First check the exact machine against the official guide for x eighty-six sixty-four computers. Look at the three checks on this card. One, the processor must be sixty-four-bit, a design almost every PC from the last ten years has. Two, the PC must start with UEFI: the built-in startup program that runs the moment you press power. You open its settings by pressing a key during startup, and many people still call it the BIOS. There, turn off Secure Boot, a feature that only lets approved operating systems start. Three, the disk must use five-hundred-and-twelve-byte logical sectors, the size of the small blocks it stores data in. Home Assistant OS cannot start from drives that only use four-kilobyte blocks. Installing replaces everything on the disk, so back up its files and write down each setting you change.

visual.title: Check the computer before changing it

check.prompt: Two spare disks: one reports 512-byte logical sectors, the other only 4096-byte sectors. Which can hold Home Assistant OS?

options.text: The 512-byte disk
options.feedback: Right. Home Assistant OS starts only from a disk with 512-byte logical sectors.

options.text: The 4096-byte disk, because bigger blocks are faster
options.feedback: Block size is a compatibility check, not a speed choice. Home Assistant OS cannot start from it.

options.text: Either disk, if Secure Boot is off
options.feedback: Secure Boot and sector size are separate checks. Only the 512-byte disk passes.

slides.title: Example: the USB stick and the disk have different jobs
body: USB stick: runs live Ubuntu for a short while
Internal disk: receives the Home Assistant OS image
slides.narration: Picture a workbench with a borrowed toolbox and a permanent cabinet. The toolbox is a USB stick of at least eight gigabytes holding live Ubuntu. Ubuntu is a free operating system. Live means it runs straight from the USB stick without being installed, and it leaves no trace when you remove the stick. The cabinet is the PC's internal disk, which will hold Home Assistant OS for good. The card shows both jobs. Start the PC from the USB stick and choose Try Ubuntu, not Install Ubuntu. Plug in an Ethernet cable, the network cable that joins the PC to your router, so Ubuntu can reach the internet. From the official Home Assistant installation page, download the Home Assistant OS disk image: one file that is an exact copy of a ready-to-run disk. The next slide restores it onto the internal disk.

visual.title: Example: the USB stick and the disk have different jobs
labels: Disk image: the copy to write

workedExample.prompt: Which device receives Home Assistant OS?
steps: Start the PC from the live Ubuntu USB stick and choose Try Ubuntu.
Identify the internal disk by name and capacity, and confirm its backup.
Check the target again at the final Restore confirmation.
workedExample.answer: The checked internal disk. Everything on it will be replaced; the USB stick only runs the tools.

check.prompt: Ubuntu offers Try Ubuntu and Install Ubuntu. Which do you choose?

options.text: Try Ubuntu
options.feedback: Right. Try Ubuntu runs from the stick and changes nothing until you restore the image yourself.

options.text: Install Ubuntu
options.feedback: That would put Ubuntu on the internal disk. You only borrow Ubuntu's tools here.

options.text: Either; they do the same thing
options.feedback: Install Ubuntu writes Ubuntu to the disk. Try Ubuntu runs it from the stick only.

slides.title: Your turn: identify both devices
body: Live USB: ___. Destination disk: ___. Backup: ___.
Disks → Restore Disk Image → check target → Restore
slides.narration: Now the step that erases the disk. In Ubuntu, open Show Applications, then the program called Disks. Select the internal disk, open the three-dot menu and choose Restore Disk Image. Pick the downloaded file, then Start Restoring. Before you press the final Restore, fill in the blanks on this card. The USB stick is this device. The destination is that disk. Its backup is stored there. Identify each one by the name and capacity shown on your screen, never by a name copied from someone else's guide. If Ubuntu reports the destination is busy, you probably started from the wrong device, so fix the startup choice. When the restore finishes, shut down and remove the USB stick when Ubuntu asks. Then set UEFI to start from the internal disk.

visual.title: Your turn: identify both devices

check.prompt: Disks shows a 16 GB USB stick and a 256 GB internal disk. Where do you restore the image?

options.text: The 256 GB internal disk
options.feedback: Right. The internal disk is the destination. The USB stick only runs Ubuntu's tools.

options.text: The 16 GB USB stick
options.feedback: The stick is the temporary toolbox. The PC must start from its internal disk afterwards.

options.text: Both, to be safe
options.feedback: Restoring onto the stick would wipe your Ubuntu tools. Choose only the internal disk.

slides.title: A capable office PC may still be unavailable
body: Current work files are not backed up
Its owner has not agreed to dedicate it
slides.narration: Now decide for a different machine. An office PC passes every hardware check from slide two. But it still holds current work files with no backup, and its owner has not agreed to give it up. The card shows the result: capable hardware and unprotected data, so you stop before erasing. First get the owner's agreement and a working backup, or choose another suitable host. While you wait, you can keep learning in the demo, the practice copy of the app from lesson A one, which runs no equipment.

visual.title: A capable office PC may still be unavailable

check.prompt: A spare PC passes every check, its owner agrees, and its files are backed up. Can you continue?

options.text: Yes. Hardware, permission and backup are all in place
options.feedback: Right. All three conditions are met, so the disk can be replaced.

options.text: No. A PC can never be dedicated
options.feedback: A PC can be dedicated once its owner agrees and its data is safe, as here.

options.text: No. Only a Raspberry Pi is supported
options.feedback: x86-64 PCs are a supported host route, alongside the Pi.

slides.title: Check first start and write down the result
body: Open http://homeassistant.local; if it fails, add :8123
Record model, disk, backup, settings, version, address
slides.narration: Start the PC from its internal disk, with the Ethernet cable plugged in, and give it a few minutes. The first start needs internet, because it downloads the latest Home Assistant. Every device on your network has a network address, like a house number on a street. Your web browser uses it to reach that device. On your everyday computer, type homeassistant dot local into the browser. If nothing opens, add colon eight one two three. That number is a port: a numbered door on the host where Home Assistant answers. When the page opens, check it is this PC. You will see onboarding: the welcome screens Home Assistant shows on first start. As the card shows, record the PC model, disk, backup location, changed settings, version and address. Lesson C three continues from onboarding.

options.text: homeassistant.local/8123
options.feedback: A port follows a colon, not a slash. Use homeassistant.local:8123.

options.text: Nothing. Restore the image again
options.feedback: Try the port address first. Check power, cable and the official guide before rewriting.

options.feedback: Right. Back up anything you need and identify the disk before you press Restore.

options.text: Its files move to the USB stick
options.feedback: Nothing is moved for you. Files you need must be backed up first.

options.text: Only browser settings change
options.feedback: The whole disk is replaced with Home Assistant OS.

quiz.prompt: With the live Ubuntu USB method, which device receives Home Assistant OS?

options.text: The checked internal destination disk
options.feedback: Right. The USB stick only runs Ubuntu's tools for a short while.

options.text: Any disk with the same name as a guide's screenshot

options.text: The live USB stick

quiz.prompt: A NUC-shaped PC is available. What must you establish?

options.text: It meets the requirements, it is dedicated, and its data is backed up

options.text: Nothing; its shape makes it supported

options.text: Use it, because the processor is suitable
options.feedback: The processor check is only one condition. Permission and backup come first.

title: Install the software and protect access
summary: Finish onboarding, install both Crop Steering parts at the same version, confirm the heartbeat and keep a backup you can restore.
outcomes: Explain entity ID, integration, Controller, HACS, app repository and heartbeat in plain words
Install the matching integration and Controller following the Crop Steering installation guide
Confirm a fresh heartbeat, your own account, the timezone and an off-host backup with its emergency kit

slides.title: Finish onboarding, then read an entity ID
body: Your own account, a private recovery note, local timezone
Entity ID = exact address, like sensor.practice_moisture
slides.narration: Your host lesson ended at onboarding: the welcome screens Home Assistant shows on its first start. Complete them now. Create your own account, meaning a username and password that belong to you alone. Write down how you would get back in if you forgot the password, and keep that recovery note private and safe. Set your timezone, the local clock region, so lights-on times match the real clock. Now recall an entity: one named reading or control inside Home Assistant. Each entity has an exact written address, called an entity ID. The card shows one: sensor dot practice underscore moisture. One probe can supply several entity IDs, for example moisture, temperature and battery. The entity ID tells software where to look, and the physical label on the probe tells you where it really is.

visual.title: Finish onboarding, then read an entity ID

check.prompt: One probe reports moisture, temperature and battery level. How many entity IDs can it create?

options.text: Three, one for each reading
options.feedback: Right. Each reading gets its own entity and its own entity ID.

options.text: One for the whole probe
options.feedback: Home Assistant names each reading separately, so one probe can give several entity IDs.

options.text: None until watering starts
options.feedback: Entities appear when the probe is added to Home Assistant. Watering has nothing to do with it.

slides.title: Two Crop Steering parts do different jobs
body: Integration: settings + screens. Controller: when to water
Same version number for both. HACS gets the integration
slides.narration: Crop Steering arrives in two parts, as lesson C one showed. The integration is the package that adds Crop Steering to Home Assistant: it stores your room settings and shows the Crop Steering screens. The Controller is a separate program that reads those settings and decides when to water. Both parts carry one version number, and you install the same number of each. This is called version matching, and it lets each part understand the other. You get the integration from HACS, short for Home Assistant Community Store: a free extra for Home Assistant that downloads community-made integrations. HACS does not install the Controller, which comes from a different place on slide four. The card shows all three pieces. Throughout setup, keep the Watering switch OFF. Remember, that switch tells the Controller whether it may start shots.

visual.title: Two Crop Steering parts do different jobs

check.prompt: HACS shows the integration at version 2.30.0. Which Controller version do you install?

options.text: 2.30.0, the same number
options.feedback: Right. Both parts carry one version number. Matching them keeps their settings readable to each other.

options.text: Any version; they are independent
options.feedback: The two parts exchange settings, so they must match. Install the same number.

options.text: The oldest available version
options.feedback: An older Controller may not understand a newer integration. Match the numbers.

slides.title: Example: install the integration and create a room
body: HACS → Download → restart Home Assistant
Setup link → manual setup → room name + zone count
slides.narration: Now install the integration, using the links in the Crop Steering installation guide. If HACS is not installed yet, install it first by following its own guide. Open the guide's HACS link for this project and select Download. Then restart Home Assistant. Restarting closes and reopens Home Assistant's software so it loads the new part, and it takes a minute or two. Next, open the guide's Crop Steering setup link. Choose manual setup, type a room name and enter how many zones the room has. For practice, the card uses a room called Practice Room with one zone. This creates the room's record in software only. The real probes and valves are connected in lesson C four.

visual.title: Example: install the integration and create a room

workedExample.prompt: What has creating Practice Room set up?
steps: Download the integration in HACS and restart Home Assistant.
Open the setup link, choose manual setup, and enter the room name and one zone.
Install the matching Controller next, on slide four.
workedExample.answer: A named room exists in software. Its probes and valves are connected in lesson C4.

check.prompt: You downloaded the integration, but the setup link cannot find Crop Steering. What did you likely skip?

options.text: Restarting Home Assistant
options.feedback: Right. Home Assistant loads new integrations when it restarts. Restart, then try the link again.

options.text: Turning Watering ON
options.feedback: Watering stays OFF during setup. A new integration needs a restart to load.

options.text: Installing a second host
options.feedback: One host is enough. The integration loads after a restart.

slides.title: Add and start the separate Controller
body: Add the app repository; install Crop Steering Controller
Same version · Start on boot on · Watchdog on · Watering OFF
slides.narration: The Controller installs from a different place, the app store. On Home Assistant OS, an app is a separate program that runs beside Home Assistant on the same host. The app store is the screen where you install apps, and it only lists apps from sources it knows. An app repository is a web address that adds another source to that list. Use the guide's Add the app repository link. Then install Crop Steering Controller at the same version as the integration. Review its options and start it, with Watering still OFF. The card shows two settings that keep it running. Start on boot starts the Controller whenever the host starts, and it is on by default. The Supervisor is the part of Home Assistant OS that manages apps. Watchdog, which you turn on, lets the Supervisor restart the Controller if it stops.

visual.title: Add and start the separate Controller

check.prompt: The Controller app stopped overnight while the host kept running. Which setting restarts it?

options.text: Watchdog
options.feedback: Right. With Watchdog on, the Supervisor restarts the app when it stops.

options.text: Start on boot
options.feedback: Start on boot acts only when the whole host starts. Watchdog covers an app that stops on its own.

options.text: The Watering switch
options.feedback: Watering decides whether shots may start. It does not restart the app.

slides.title: Your turn: the screens open but no heartbeat arrives
body: Heartbeat = the Controller's regular I-am-running message
Screens but no heartbeat: check the Controller app
slides.narration: Open Crop Steering in the Home Assistant sidebar, the menu down the left side of the screen. Next, check that the Controller is talking. A running Controller regularly sends Home Assistant a short status message saying it is alive. This message is called the heartbeat. Its age tells you how recently the Controller reported, as a reading's age did in lesson A six. The Controller sends it using an access key that the Supervisor hands over automatically, so you never type or paste one. Now the case on the card: the Crop Steering screens open, but no heartbeat arrives. The screens come from the integration, so check the Controller app. Is it installed, started and at the same version? If an older Controller already runs this room, finish its documented upgrade first, so that one Controller owns the room.

visual.title: Your turn: the screens open but no heartbeat arrives

check.prompt: The Crop Steering screens work, but the heartbeat age reads three hours. What does that tell you?

options.text: The Controller stopped reporting; check its app
options.feedback: Right. The screens come from the integration. An old heartbeat points at the Controller app.

options.text: The integration failed; download it again
options.feedback: The screens open, so the integration works. The heartbeat comes from the Controller.

options.text: Nothing; heartbeats only arrive during shots
options.feedback: A running Controller sends its heartbeat regularly, shots or not. Three hours old means it stopped.

slides.title: Keep a recovery copy you can actually use
body: Settings → System → Backups; keep a copy off the host
Save the emergency kit: it holds the encryption key
slides.narration: Last, make a way back. A backup is a saved copy of your Home Assistant setup that can rebuild it on new hardware. Make one in Settings, then System, then Backups. Home Assistant normally encrypts backups: it locks them with an encryption key, a long code needed to open them. It offers that key as a download called the emergency kit. As the card shows, keep the emergency kit and a backup copy away from this host. A USB stick in a drawer works. A backup kept only on the host is lost if its storage fails. Finally, compare Home Assistant's clock with your phone. Then move on to lesson C four, with Watering still OFF.

visual.title: Keep a recovery copy you can actually use

check.prompt: Your backup file is on a USB stick, but the emergency kit is lost. Can you restore it?

options.text: No. The kit holds the key that opens the backup
options.feedback: Right. An encrypted backup needs its key. Store the kit safely, away from the host.

options.text: Yes. The file alone is enough
options.feedback: An encrypted backup cannot be opened without its encryption key.

options.text: Yes, if the clock is correct
options.feedback: The clock has nothing to do with it. Opening the backup needs the key in the emergency kit.

practice.prompt: Prepare a software record with both installed version numbers, the room name, the heartbeat age, how you would recover your account, and where the backup copy and emergency kit are kept.
hints: HACS download, room setup and the Controller app install are separate steps.
An encrypted backup needs its emergency kit to open.
practice.success: The record shows matching version numbers, the intended room, a fresh heartbeat, an account-recovery method and an off-host backup with its emergency kit.

quiz.prompt: What does HACS download in this course's route?

options.text: The integration; the Controller comes from the app store
options.feedback: Right. HACS, the setup link and the app store are three separate steps.

options.text: Both parts and every connected device
options.feedback: HACS gets only the integration. The Controller comes from the app store, and devices are added separately.

options.text: Firmware for every sensor
options.feedback: HACS downloads Home Assistant integrations. Probe firmware comes from the probe maker.

quiz.prompt: The Crop Steering screens open, but there is no fresh heartbeat. What next?

options.text: Check the Controller is installed, started and the same version, with Watering OFF
options.feedback: Right. The screens come from the integration; the heartbeat comes from the Controller.

options.text: Turn Watering ON to force a heartbeat
options.feedback: Watering does not start a stopped app, and it must stay OFF until checks pass.

options.text: Assume the screens prove the Controller works
options.feedback: The screens come from the integration. Only a fresh heartbeat shows the Controller is running.

quiz.prompt: What is an entity ID?

options.text: The exact written address of one reading or control
options.feedback: Right. Check its units and the probe's physical label separately.

options.text: Proof that a valve is wired correctly
options.feedback: An entity ID is a software address. Wiring is checked physically.

options.text: The serial number of a whole device
options.feedback: One device can have several entity IDs, one per reading or control.

quiz.prompt: The only backup is on the host's storage, which just failed. Can you recover?

options.text: No. You need a copy off the host and its emergency kit
options.feedback: Right. Keep a backup copy and the emergency kit somewhere other than the host.

options.text: Yes. A screenshot of the finished backup is enough
options.feedback: A screenshot is not the backup file. Recovery needs the file and its key.

options.text: Yes. Setting the timezone restores the files
options.feedback: The timezone sets the clock. It does not restore anything.

Prepare a software record with both installed version numbers, the room name, the heartbeat age, how you would recover your account, and where the backup copy and emergency kit are kept.
For a real installation, keep Watering OFF and pumps and valves disconnected, follow the Crop Steering installation guide and record what you checked and anything still unresolved.

title: Tell the software which zone is which
summary: Map one zone's probes and valve, enter per-plant sizing, and wait for the Controller's Mapping acknowledged receipt with Watering OFF.

slides.title: A contact name needs the right number
body: Mapping = telling Crop Steering which entities a zone uses
Add devices to Home Assistant first; then Equipment → Setup
slides.narration: A phone contact can have the right name and still dial the wrong number. Software works the same way. Mapping means telling Crop Steering which Home Assistant entities belong to each zone: this probe, this valve. First add each probe and valve control to Home Assistant through its own supported setup, because Crop Steering only maps entities that already exist. Check each entity ID, the exact written address from lesson C three, against the physical label on the equipment, as the card shows. Then open Crop Steering, select the room, and open the Equipment menu, then Setup. Keep the Watering switch OFF, so the Controller starts no shots, and keep the physical shutdowns your installer set up in place.

visual.alt: Actual isolated demo screen. Read the displayed room and current sample values; separate paper examples use fictional values.

check.prompt: A new probe is not in Home Assistant yet. Can you map it in Crop Steering?

options.text: No. Add it to Home Assistant first
options.feedback: Right. Setup maps entities that already exist; it does not add devices.

options.text: Yes. Setup finds and adds it
options.feedback: Setup only lists existing entities. Add the probe through its own Home Assistant setup first.

options.text: Yes, after turning Watering ON
options.feedback: Watering stays OFF, and it does not add devices. Add the probe to Home Assistant first.

slides.title: Match the real plumbing and measurements
body: Supply type: Zone valves only OR A pump, then zone valves
Probes: VWC in percent, recent last update, EC type known
slides.narration: Setup asks how water reaches the room, called the supply type. Choose Zone valves only when each zone valve is fed straight from a pressurised supply. Choose A pump, then zone valves when water flows only while a pump runs. Map a pump only if one really exists, and give every zone its own valve. Then look at the probes, as on this screen. Check two things for each moisture probe. First the units: VWC should read in percent. Second the last update: the time of its newest reading, which should be recent. For each EC probe, note whether it gives feed, bulk or pore-water EC. If an optional reading does not exist, leave it unmapped rather than borrowing another number.

visual.title: Match the real plumbing and measurements
visual.alt: Actual isolated demo screen. Read the displayed room and current sample values; separate paper examples use fictional values.

check.prompt: A small room has one zone valve fed straight from a building's water pipe. There is no pump. Which supply type?

options.text: Zone valves only
options.feedback: Right. The pressurised supply feeds the valve directly, so no pump is mapped.

options.text: A pump, then zone valves
options.feedback: That type needs a real pump to map. This room has none.

options.text: Leave the supply type blank
options.feedback: Setup needs the answer and does not guess. Choose Zone valves only.

slides.title: Example: twelve plants, not one giant pot
body: 12 plants · 3 L substrate per plant · 2 drippers per plant
3 L/h per dripper → 12 × 2 × 3 = 72 L/h zone delivery
slides.narration: Next comes sizing: the numbers that turn runtime into litres. Setup asks for four numbers per zone, and all except the plant count are per plant. Imagine twelve plants, each in three litres of substrate, each with two drippers measured at three litres per hour. Enter plant count twelve, substrate per plant three litres, drippers per plant two, and flow per dripper three litres per hour. The card shows the zone delivery. Twelve plants times two drippers is twenty-four drippers. Twenty-four times three litres per hour is seventy-two litres per hour. Keep the per-plant box at three litres, not thirty-six. Thirty-six litres is the zone's total substrate, and it would tell the software each plant has a giant pot.

visual.title: Example: twelve plants, not one giant pot

workedExample.prompt: Estimate delivery for 12 plants with 2 drippers each, measured at 3 L/h per dripper.
steps: 12 × 2 = 24 drippers.
24 × 3 = 72 L/h estimated zone delivery.
Enter substrate as 3 L per plant, not the 36 L total.
workedExample.answer: 72 L/h zone delivery. It describes water supplied, not water taken up by the plants.

check.prompt: Six plants each sit in 4 L of substrate. What goes in substrate per plant?

options.text: 4 L
options.feedback: Right. The box is per plant. The software multiplies by the plant count itself.
24 L is the zone total, 6 × 4. The box asks for one plant's substrate.

options.text: 6 L
options.feedback: 6 is the plant count. Enter each plant's substrate, 4 L.

slides.title: Check the clock and the receipt
body: Lights-on and lights-off hours must match the real timer
Review → Save → wait for Mapping acknowledged
slides.narration: Two checks come before saving. First the clock. Write down the timezone, the room's lights-on and lights-off hours in Crop Steering, and the times on the real light timer. They must agree, because Crop Steering does not switch the lights; it only uses those hours to plan the day. Second, the receipt. Choose Review configuration, read the list of changes and problems, then choose Save configuration. Each save creates a new revision: a numbered edition of the setup. Saving is like posting a letter. The Controller then reads the new revision and sends back an acknowledgement, its receipt, which the card shows as Mapping acknowledged. Wait for that receipt for this revision. A fresh heartbeat shows the Controller is alive, and only the acknowledgement shows it accepted your setup.

visual.title: Check the clock and the receipt

check.prompt: Setup was saved a minute ago. The heartbeat is fresh, but Mapping acknowledged has not appeared. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for the acknowledgement, with Watering OFF
options.feedback: Right. Saved and accepted are separate. Only the receipt shows the Controller took this revision.

options.text: Treat the fresh heartbeat as the receipt
options.feedback: The heartbeat says the Controller is alive, not that it accepted this revision.

options.text: Turn Watering ON to speed it up
options.feedback: Watering stays OFF. It does not make the Controller accept a revision.

slides.title: Your turn: three faults in one record
body: 8 × 1 × 2.5 = 20 L/h: the arithmetic is right
Faults: wrong-room probe, blank lights hours, no receipt
slides.narration: Now review a record yourself. Eight plants, four litres per plant, one dripper each, measured at two point five litres per hour. Eight plants times one dripper is eight drippers. Eight times two point five litres per hour is twenty litres per hour. The arithmetic is right, but the card shows three faults. The moisture entity belongs to the next room. The lights-on and lights-off hours are blank. And the revision is saved but not acknowledged. Each fault must be fixed before Watering can be turned on. You can practise this kind of review in the demo, with no equipment connected.

visual.title: Your turn: three faults in one record

check.prompt: Ten plants have two drippers each, measured at 1.5 L/h per dripper. What is the zone delivery?

options.text: 30 L/h
options.feedback: Right. 10 × 2 = 20 drippers, and 20 × 1.5 = 30 L/h.

options.text: 15 L/h
options.feedback: That uses one dripper per plant. Multiply by 2 drippers first: 20 × 1.5 = 30 L/h.

options.text: 3 L/h
options.feedback: That is two drippers on one plant. Multiply by all 10 plants: 30 L/h.

slides.title: Read the accepted setup back
body: Check Status → Room and Equipment → Probes
Unknown is not OFF. Watering stays OFF until C5 and C6
slides.narration: After the acknowledgement arrives, read the setup back. Open Overview, the main status screen, then Selected room, its view of one room. Next open Equipment, then Probes. Compare each reading, its units and its age with your written setup sheet. Check the sizing, the measured flow, the light hours and the one owner of each output. A state that reads unknown means the software cannot tell, so treat it as a fault to fix, not as OFF. The card shows the accepted revision and the live values. Lesson C five checks the physical protections, and lesson C six proves the water starts and stops. Until those pass with the responsible people present, Watering stays OFF.

options.feedback: Right. Unknown means the software cannot tell. Find out why before going further.

options.text: As OFF, since nothing is running
options.feedback: Unknown is not a reading of OFF. The valve could be in any state.

options.text: As ON, to be careful
options.feedback: Guessing either way hides the fault. Fix the reading so the state is known.

options.feedback: Right. The entity ID must match the physical probe in this zone.

options.text: Use it because the name sounds right

options.text: Average it with the tank temperature

options.text: 40 L/h

options.text: 4 L/h
options.feedback: That is one plant's two drippers. Multiply by all 10 plants: 40 L/h.

options.text: 20 L/h
options.feedback: 20 is the dripper count. Multiply by 2 L/h each: 40 L/h.

quiz.prompt: The Home Assistant timezone is correct. What still needs checking?

options.text: The room's lights hours against the real light timer
options.feedback: Right. Crop Steering plans by those hours but does not switch the lights.

options.text: Nothing; the timezone sets every light
options.feedback: The timezone sets the clock. The lights follow their own timer.

options.text: Only the browser theme
options.feedback: The theme changes colours. The lights hours must match the real timer.

quiz.prompt: Setup is saved and the heartbeat is fresh, but there is no Mapping acknowledged. Ready to water?

options.text: No. Keep Watering OFF until the acknowledgement arrives
options.feedback: Right. Saved and accepted are separate states. Wait for the receipt.

options.text: Yes. Saved and accepted mean the same
options.feedback: Saving stores the setup. Only the acknowledgement shows the Controller took it.

options.text: Yes. Watering will force acceptance

title: Make the physical equipment safe to test
summary: Learn what the Watering switch can and cannot stop, check how each probe and pump is connected, and give every output one controller before any water flows.
outcomes: Explain why Watering OFF is a software block, not physical isolation
Check a probe's supply voltage, signal protocol, firmware and interface against its documentation
Record ratings, protections, physical shutdown and one owner for every output before the wet test

slides.title: Watering OFF is a software block, not isolation
body: Watering OFF: the Controller starts no shots
Isolation: power and water cut off by real devices
Agree the physical shutdown and who controls it
slides.narration: Think of a stop request to a bus driver. Only that driver hears it. Crop Steering’s Watering switch works like that request. Each room has a Watering switch at the top of its screen, and you have kept it OFF since lesson C three. When Watering is OFF, the Controller starts no shots in that room. That includes rescue shots and test shots. A test shot is a shot you ask the app to run on demand. A shot that is already running stops within a few seconds. That is a software block. It does not cut electricity, and it cannot stop an old timer or a hand switch. Physical isolation means cutting power or water with a real device. Examples are a switch that cuts the electricity supply, or a closed hand valve on the water line. Electrical isolation is the power part of that. Look at the cues on screen. Before anyone works on a pump, valve or wiring, agree the approved electrical and water shutdown, and who controls it. Next, you check how each probe connects.

visual.title: A stop message is not a disconnected machine

check.prompt: Watering is OFF for Room A. An old timer is still wired to the Zone 1 valve. What can still open that valve?

options.text: The old timer
options.feedback: Right. Watering OFF only stops the Crop Steering Controller. The timer is a separate route to water.

options.text: Nothing; Watering OFF blocks every device
options.feedback: Watering OFF blocks Controller shots only. Timers and hand switches still work.

options.text: Only a Crop Steering rescue shot
options.feedback: Watering OFF blocks rescue shots too. The timer is the route that remains.

slides.title: Use the probe’s documented connection
body: Check supply voltage, signal protocol, firmware, interface
Never guess a wire’s job from its colour
First install: choose a documented, assembled route
slides.narration: A plug that fits is like an envelope that fits a letterbox. The letter inside can still be wrong. So you check four things before you connect a probe. Supply voltage is the electrical push the probe needs to run, measured in volts. Too much can destroy it. The signal protocol is the wiring language from lesson C one: how the probe sends its readings. The interface is whatever the probe plugs into. Often that is a bridge, the translator box. The interface must speak the probe’s language. Firmware is the small program built into the probe or bridge. Some probes need a particular firmware version. Look at the cues on screen. For example, before you connect a TEROS twelve, read its maker’s sheet. Confirm its voltage, protocol and the bridges it supports. Then follow its placement and calibration steps. Never guess a wire’s job from its colour, and never connect an unknown signal straight to the metal pins on a computer board. For a first install, choose a documented, assembled route. Next, check that a working reading measures the right thing.

visual.title: Use the probe’s documented connection

check.prompt: A new probe’s plug fits your bridge, but its sheet lists a supply voltage the bridge does not provide. What do you do?

options.text: Stop and find an interface the probe’s documents support
options.feedback: Right. A fitting plug says nothing about voltage or protocol. Use a documented match.

options.text: Connect it, because the plug fits
options.feedback: Plugs can fit while the voltage is wrong. The wrong voltage can destroy the probe.

options.text: Swap wires by colour until a reading appears
options.feedback: Colours do not define a wire’s job. Guessing can damage the probe or the bridge.

slides.title: Example: a number can be fresh and irrelevant
body: Fresh 22 °C tank reading is not zone moisture
Check quantity, units, real location and age together
Bulk EC does not become pore-water EC by renaming
slides.narration: A reading can be recent and still answer the wrong question. Picture a thermometer hanging in the tank, not in the pot. Here is a made-up example. Remember: an entity is one named reading or control inside Home Assistant. This entity shows twenty-two. It updated two minutes ago, so it is fresh. Its name mentions Room A. But its unit is degrees Celsius, and the sensor sits in the tank. Moisture in Room A is VWC, a percentage of the substrate’s volume, measured in the pot. So this number cannot stand in for moisture. Look at the three labels on screen. Check four things together: quantity, units, real location and age. The same care applies to EC. Remember from lesson A five: bulk EC is measured through the substrate. Pore-water EC describes the water between the pieces. A bulk EC reading does not become pore-water EC because a field asks for it. A wrong reading makes the Controller water for the wrong reason. Next, look at the pump.

visual.title: Example: a number can be fresh and irrelevant
visual.alt: Actual isolated demo screen. Read the displayed room and current sample values; separate paper examples use fictional values.

workedExample.prompt: Can a fresh 22 °C tank reading fill Room A’s moisture field?
steps: Quantity and units: temperature in °C, not VWC in %.
Location: the tank, not the substrate in Room A’s pots.
Choose the verified moisture entity from the probe in the pot instead.
workedExample.answer: No. A fresh tank temperature is not substrate moisture.

check.prompt: An entity named Room A EC reads 1.8 mS/cm, updated a minute ago. It measures the feed tank. Can it fill Room A’s pore-water EC field?

options.text: No; it measures feed in the tank, not water in the pot
options.feedback: Right. Location and method matter. Feed EC is not pore-water EC.

options.text: Yes; the units are mS/cm
options.feedback: Matching units do not make the same measurement. Check where and how it was measured.

options.text: Yes; it is fresh
options.feedback: Freshness shows the reading is recent. It does not show what or where it measures.

slides.title: Check what starts and stops the pump
body: Pumps draw a surge at start-up: the starting load
A competent installer checks ratings and protection
Plan for dry-run, deadheading, backflow and siphon
slides.narration: Remember from lesson C one: a pump draws a burst of extra power as it starts, like the shove that gets a loaded trolley rolling. That burst is the starting load. A rating is the most a device is designed to handle safely. It is printed on its label. A smart plug’s headline rating usually describes a heater, not a motor. A competent installer is a qualified person, such as a licensed electrician or plumber. That person checks the real pump, its control hardware, the ratings and the protection it needs. Mains is the high-voltage power behind your wall sockets, and this course gives no mains-wiring instructions. The installer also plans for faults. Dry-run means the pump runs with no water and overheats. Deadheading means the pump pushes against a closed valve, with nowhere for water to go. Backflow and siphon, from lesson C one, mean water running backwards or draining on its own. Look at the cues on screen. Before any test, agree what will be energised, meaning receive power, where water comes out, and how the test ends. Next, find any second controller.

visual.title: Check what starts and stops the pump

check.prompt: Your pump runs from a smart plug whose label gives a rating for heaters. Is that label enough to approve it for the pump?

options.text: No; a competent installer checks the motor’s starting load
options.feedback: Right. A heater rating does not cover a motor’s start-up burst. The installer decides.

options.text: Yes; the pump is small, so any plug will do
options.feedback: Even a small motor draws a burst at start-up. Only an installer can approve the match.

options.text: Yes, if the dashboard shows it switching
options.feedback: A switching icon proves communication, not a safe electrical rating.

slides.title: Your turn: two controllers know the same valve
body: Old timer can still open the valve
Watering OFF does not stop the timer
Give each output one owner before testing
slides.narration: Two people steering one car is dangerous, even when one of them is resting. A valve works the same way. Here is the case. An old timer is still wired to a valve. You have also mapped that valve into Crop Steering, and Watering is OFF. Remember from lesson C four: mapping tells Crop Steering which entity is which valve. The old timer is a competing controller, a second system that can also open the valve. Look at the comparison on screen. The left side can still act. The right side is OFF, but that does not stop the left. So the valve is not isolated. Write down both routes to water. Then choose one owner for the output, and have the installer disable or remove the other route. Crop Steering may still do read-only observation. That means it reads values but sends no commands. Agree how the plants still get water while you sort this out. Two owners can fight, double-water or leave a valve open. Next, close the physical checks.

visual.title: Your turn: two controllers know the same valve
visual.alt: The old timer and new Controller must not both own an output.

check.prompt: An older Home Assistant automation also switches your Zone 1 valve. Crop Steering will own it. What happens before testing?

options.text: Disable or remove the automation so one controller owns the valve
options.feedback: Right. One owner per output. The old automation could open the valve at any time.

options.text: Keep both; the faster one wins
options.feedback: Two controllers can fight or double-water. Remove one route first.

options.text: Leave it; Watering OFF overrides it
options.feedback: Watering OFF only blocks Crop Steering. The automation still works.

slides.title: Close the physical checks before the wet test
body: Trace each probe and each output to real equipment
Record ratings, protections, owner and shutdown
Go to C6 only with an approved catch-test plan
slides.narration: Before you leave a house, you check the doors, the oven and the taps. This slide is that last walk round. A wet test is the first time water really flows through the new system. First, trace each probe to its Home Assistant reading. Then trace each control entity back to the real valve or pump. Where the design allows, the installer confirms each output with a low-risk indicator, such as a small lamp, in place of the real load. Never use a live crop as the first wiring test. Look at the three cues on screen. Then write the setup record: interface, ratings, protections, one owner and the physical shutdown. For example: Zone one valve, owned by Crop Steering, old timer removed, water shutdown at the labelled hand valve. An open question keeps this stage unfinished. Move to lesson C six only with an approved catch-test method and safe collection ready. Lesson C six runs that first careful water test.

visual.title: Close the physical checks before the wet test

check.prompt: Your record lists probes, ratings and owners, but the physical shutdown line is blank. Can you start C6?

options.text: No; agree and record the physical shutdown first
options.feedback: Right. Everyone must know how to stop real water and power before it flows.

options.text: Yes; the Watering switch is the shutdown
options.feedback: Watering OFF is a software block. A physical shutdown cuts real power or water.

options.text: Yes; fill it in after the test
options.feedback: You need the shutdown during the test, in case water does not stop.

practice.prompt: Explain the old-timer conflict in your own words. Then fill in a physical setup record for one zone: probe interface, output owner, ratings, protections and physical shutdown.
hints: Watering OFF blocks the Controller only. Name every other route that can open the valve.
For each line, write who checked it. Mark anything unchecked as unresolved.
practice.success: The record names one owner per output, the competent installer’s rating and protection checks, and an agreed physical shutdown. Any blank line keeps C6 on hold.

quiz.prompt: Watering is OFF, but an old timer can still open the valve. What is true?

options.text: The valve is not isolated and has two owners
options.feedback: Right. Watering OFF blocks Crop Steering only. Remove the second owner and use physical isolation for work.

options.text: Watering OFF disables the old timer too
options.feedback: Watering OFF never reaches other controllers. The timer still runs on its own.

options.text: The valve is safe to work on because the screen shows OFF
options.feedback: A screen shows software state. Before work, cut power and water with the agreed physical shutdown.

quiz.prompt: A probe plug fits a bridge. Is that enough to connect it?

options.text: No; check supply voltage, signal protocol, firmware and interface
options.feedback: Right. Read the probe’s documents and confirm each item before you connect.

options.text: Yes; matching plugs mean matching signals
options.feedback: Plugs can match while the voltage or protocol differs. That can destroy the probe.

options.text: Yes; copy the wire colours from a similar probe
options.feedback: Colours do not define a wire’s job. Use the exact probe’s documentation.

quiz.prompt: A fresh entity shows tank temperature in °C. Can it fill Room A’s VWC field?

options.text: No; the quantity, units and location are all wrong
options.feedback: Right. VWC is moisture in the pot, as a percentage. This is temperature in the tank.

options.text: Yes; it updated recently
options.feedback: Fresh means recent. It still has to measure the right thing in the right place.

options.text: Yes, after renaming it to moisture
options.feedback: A new name does not move the sensor or change what it measures.

quiz.prompt: Who confirms that the pump’s switching hardware and protections are suitable?

options.text: A competent installer, using the real ratings and site rules
options.feedback: Right. Starting load, dry-run and deadheading protection need a qualified, site-specific check.

options.text: Passing this quiz
options.feedback: The quiz checks understanding. It cannot inspect real equipment.

options.text: Any dashboard that shows an OFF icon
options.feedback: An icon reports software state. It says nothing about ratings or protection.

title: First water: catch it, measure it, stop it
summary: Commission one zone in two stages: an installer-run equipment test with Watering OFF, then a supervised Controller cycle once every readiness check passes.
outcomes: Explain the two commissioning stages and why Watering stays OFF in stage one
Turn a timed catch in millilitres into litres per hour, and spot uneven delivery
Use the readiness checklist, then supervise and record the first enabled cycle

slides.title: Two tests answer two questions
body: Commissioning: prove each part works before relying on it
Stage one: equipment test, Watering stays OFF
Stage two: supervised Controller cycle, after readiness
slides.narration: Before a new building opens, someone checks the pipes and the wiring. For your system, that check is called commissioning. It means proving each part works safely before you rely on it. It has two stages. Look at the cues on screen. Stage one is the equipment test. It asks: does water go where it should, and does it stop? Stage two is the supervised Controller cycle. It asks: does Crop Steering water correctly on its own while someone watches? In stage one, the Watering switch stays OFF. Remember from lesson C five: OFF blocks every Controller shot, test shots included. So the competent installer runs the valve or pump with the maker’s approved procedure. The test has a bounded duration, meaning a fixed length of time agreed in advance. For example, thirty seconds, with cups under the drippers and the physical shutdown within reach. Next, watch the whole water path.

visual.title: Two tests answer two questions

check.prompt: Stage one is about to start. Someone suggests turning Watering ON to fire a test shot. What is right?

options.text: Keep Watering OFF; the installer runs the approved equipment procedure
options.feedback: Right. Stage one tests the water path itself, with the Controller blocked.

options.text: Turn Watering ON briefly, since it is only a test
options.feedback: Watering ON lets the Controller start any shot that is due, rescue shots included. That is stage two.

options.text: Work round the Watering switch in Home Assistant
options.feedback: Never bypass the block. Ask the installer for an approved equipment procedure instead.

slides.title: Watch the whole water path
body: Remove only the isolation this test needs
One catch cup per dripper, timed with a stopwatch
Watch the drippers until the water really stops
slides.narration: Picture filling a bath while you check every other tap in the house. You want one tap running and no others. With the installer present, remove only the isolation this one test needs. Leave everything else shut off. Look at the diagram on screen. Water flows from the supply, through the valve, to the drippers. Remember from lesson B four: a dripper is a small tap at each plant. Place a catch cup, a small measuring cup, under several drippers. Use one cup per dripper, not one cup for all. Time the run with a stopwatch. While it runs, watch three things. The intended drippers should flow. Other zones should stay dry. The pump and valve should switch in the agreed order. Then stop the test the agreed way, and keep watching the drippers until the water stops. Also check for siphon, from lesson C one: water that keeps draining after the stop. A screen icon reports what the software sent, so your eyes on the dripper are the proof. Next, turn a cup into a number.

visual.title: Watch the whole water path
visual.alt: Timed individual catches, observed stopping and a checked water path.

check.prompt: After the stop, the valve icon turns grey, but one dripper keeps dribbling for a minute. What do you record?

options.text: Water did not stop; investigate siphon or the valve before going on
options.feedback: Right. The dripper is the evidence. Find the cause and retest.

options.text: Stopped, because the icon is grey
options.feedback: The icon shows the command sent. The dripper shows what the water did.

options.text: Nothing; one minute is too short to matter
options.feedback: Water that keeps flowing after a stop is a fault. It can overwater or drain a tank.

slides.title: Example: a cup becomes a flow measurement
body: Separate cups: 30, 33, 37 mL = 3.6, 3.96, 4.44 L/h
slides.narration: A cup tells you millilitres in a number of seconds. Your setup from lesson C four asks for litres per hour, written L slash h. Here is how to convert, step by step. Suppose one dripper fills its cup with thirty millilitres in thirty seconds. Step one: change millilitres to litres. Thirty divided by one thousand is zero point zero three litres. Step two: scale up to an hour. An hour has three thousand six hundred seconds. Zero point zero three times three thousand six hundred is one hundred and eight. Step three: divide by the thirty seconds the test ran. One hundred and eight divided by thirty is three point six. So this dripper delivers three point six litres per hour. Look at the three steps on screen. Now say three cups held thirty, thirty-three and thirty-seven millilitres. They work out to three point six, three point nine six and four point four four litres per hour. One total would hide that difference. These are example numbers, so never enter them for a real zone. Next, you try one yourself.

visual.title: Example: a cup becomes a flow measurement

workedExample.prompt: Convert 30 mL caught in 30 seconds into L/h.
steps: 108 ÷ 30 s of runtime = 3.6.
Record the dripper, runtime and test conditions beside the result.
workedExample.answer: 3.6 L/h for that dripper during this catch.

check.prompt: A dripper fills its cup with 25 mL in 30 seconds. What is its flow?

options.text: 25 L/h
options.feedback: That skips the conversion. Change mL to litres, scale to an hour, then divide by seconds.
25 ÷ 30 gives mL per second. You still need to scale to an hour and convert to litres.

slides.title: Your turn: finish the catch record
body: Uneven delivery: find the cause, fix it, catch again
Never fake a fault by pulling wires or power
slides.narration: Now you try it. A dripper fills twenty-four millilitres in thirty seconds. Pause and work it out. Twenty-four divided by one thousand is zero point zero two four litres. Times three thousand six hundred is eighty-six point four. Divided by thirty is two point eight eight litres per hour. Write that on the record with the dripper, the runtime and the conditions. Look at the cues on screen. Suppose its neighbours gave about three point six. That gap is uneven delivery, meaning some plants get less water than others. Look for a clog, a leak or low pressure. Fix it, then repeat the catch. Then the installer tests the independent protections, such as dry-run protection, with the maker’s method. Remember from lesson C five: deadheading means a pump pushing against a closed valve. Never fake a fault by pulling wires or power while the pump runs, or by shutting valves against it. That can wreck the pump or flood the room. Next, decide whether a good catch is enough.

visual.title: Your turn: finish the catch record

check.prompt: Four drippers measure 3.6, 3.5, 3.7 and 1.9 L/h. What do you do?

options.text: Inspect the 1.9 L/h dripper, fix it and repeat the catch
options.feedback: Right. That plant gets about half the water. Find the clog, leak or pressure fault.

options.text: Average the four and move on
options.feedback: An average hides the plant that is short of water. Investigate the low dripper.

options.text: Lengthen the runtime for the whole zone
options.feedback: That overwaters the other plants and leaves the fault in place. Fix the cause.

slides.title: A good catch is one part of readiness
body: Readiness checklist: every item must pass
Saved but not acknowledged: keep Watering OFF
Enter measured flow, then wait for the receipt
slides.narration: A pilot runs a whole checklist, not only the fuel check. Your system needs the same. The readiness checklist is the list of checks that must all pass before stage two. Look at the cues on screen. The items are: correct room and outputs, fresh probe readings and acknowledged mapping. Then measured flow, water seen stopping and tested protections. Then lights-on and lights-off hours, timezone, approved local targets and recovery access. Remember from lesson C four: acknowledgement is the Controller’s receipt for a saved setup. Now decide a case. The catch and the stop both passed. You entered the measured flow and pressed Save configuration. But Mapping acknowledged has not appeared. Keep Watering OFF. Find out why the Controller has not accepted the revision, fix it and wait for the receipt. Turning Watering on will not repair a setup problem. Next, the first supervised cycle.

visual.title: A good catch is one part of readiness

check.prompt: Every readiness item passes except the room’s lights-on and lights-off hours, which are blank. Can stage two start?

options.text: No; enter and check the hours against the real lights first
options.feedback: Right. The phases follow lights-on and lights-off. Blank hours mean wrong timing.

options.text: Yes; lighting does not affect watering
options.feedback: It does. From B2, each phase is timed from lights-on and lights-off.

options.text: Yes; the catch test passed
options.feedback: A good catch is one item. Every item must pass.

slides.title: Supervise the first enabled cycle
body: Operator turns Watering ON for the selected room
Watch the shot, the stop and the event record
Water won’t stop: physical shutdown first, then OFF
slides.narration: A learner driver’s first trip has an instructor in the next seat. Stage two is that first trip. Once every readiness item passes, the responsible operator turns Watering ON for the selected room. Enabling Watering lets Crop Steering start any shot it decides is due, including rescue shots. So this is real watering, not a harmless check. Use approved local settings, not this course’s example numbers. Keep the catch cups and the shutdown ready. Look at the cues on screen. Watch the right drippers run, other zones stay dry and the water stop. Then check the event record, which lists shots that happened. Check the next action, the Controller’s note of what it plans next. If water keeps flowing when it should not, use the physical shutdown first. Then turn Watering OFF. Write down what happened and the agreed final state, for example Watering ON, with the operator checking each shot today. Repeat both stages for each new output. After the quiz, lesson C seven shows how to move zones over from an older controller, one at a time.

visual.title: Supervise the first enabled cycle

check.prompt: During stage two, a valve keeps running after the shot should have ended. What do you do first?

options.text: Use the physical shutdown, then turn Watering OFF
options.feedback: Right. Stop the real water first. Then block the Controller and investigate.

options.text: Turn Watering OFF and wait to see
options.feedback: Watering OFF is a software block. If the valve is stuck, only the physical shutdown stops water.

options.text: Lower the moisture target
options.feedback: Targets change future decisions. They do not stop water already flowing.

practice.prompt: Calculate the flow for 18 mL caught in 20 seconds. Then review a setup that is saved but not acknowledged, and write your stage-two decision and final-state record.
hints: 18 mL = 0.018 L. Multiply by 3600, then divide by 20 seconds.
Stage two needs acknowledged mapping as well as every physical and software readiness item.
practice.success: 0.018 × 3600 ÷ 20 = 3.24 L/h. Keep Watering OFF until Mapping acknowledged appears. Record the real delivery, the observed stop and the agreed final state.

quiz.prompt: Watering is OFF. Can a Crop Steering test shot run for stage one?

options.text: No; stage one uses the installer’s approved equipment procedure
options.feedback: Right. OFF blocks ordinary, rescue and test shots. Never bypass it.

options.text: Yes; test shots ignore Watering OFF
options.feedback: Test shots are blocked too. That is why the installer runs stage one.

options.text: Yes; the demo’s test button runs the real valve
options.feedback: The demo is a practice copy that runs no equipment.

quiz.prompt: A dripper fills its cup with 40 mL in 40 seconds. What is its flow?

options.text: 40 L/h
options.feedback: That skips the conversion. Change mL to litres, multiply by 3600, then divide by 40.

options.text: 1 L/h
options.feedback: 40 ÷ 40 is mL per second. Scale to an hour and convert: 1 mL/s = 3.6 L/h.

quiz.prompt: The screen says OFF, but water keeps flowing. What do you do?

options.text: Use the agreed physical shutdown, then find the fault
options.feedback: Right. Real flowing water outranks what a screen says.

options.text: Wait for the icon to change again
options.feedback: Waiting lets water keep flowing. Stop it physically first.

options.text: Lower the moisture target
options.feedback: A target changes future shots. It cannot stop water already flowing.

quiz.prompt: When may the first supervised stage-two cycle begin?

options.text: After every software and physical readiness item passes
options.feedback: Right. Then the operator enables Watering with approved settings, supervision and shutdown ready.

options.text: As soon as one catch succeeds
options.feedback: A catch is one item. Mapping, readings, timing, targets and protections must pass too.

options.text: When the Crop Steering workspace opens
options.feedback: An open page shows the software runs. It proves nothing about water or setup.

instructions: First work the 18 mL example on paper, or practise in the demo, which runs no equipment.
Calculate the flow for 18 mL in 20 seconds, review a setup that is saved but not acknowledged, and write your stage-two decision and final-state record.
For real equipment, work only with the competent installer, the installation’s approved procedure and the agreed physical shutdown. Record what was checked and what is still unresolved.
