title: Move from Growlink one zone at a time
summary: Record what your existing Growlink system does, then hand over one zone at a time, with one controller per output and a checked way back.
outcomes: Record one existing Growlink zone: equipment, settings, timing and owner
Plan a handover with one controller per output, crop-care cover and a rollback
Prove one moved zone with C6 commissioning before moving the next

slides.title: Moving house starts with a labelled inventory
body: Growlink: an existing commercial irrigation controller
Migration: moving control from one system to another
Start by observing one room and one zone
slides.narration: Before you move house, you label every box while it is still in the old house. This lesson is about that kind of move. Growlink is a commercial irrigation controller sold by another company. Some growers already water with it. Migration means moving control of your watering from one system to another, here from Growlink to Crop Steering. If you have no Growlink system, follow along on paper. Look at the cues on screen. First, observe and change nothing. Pick one room and one zone. Write down its probes, valves, pump and the controller in charge today. Also write who runs it and who can recover it if it fails. For example: Room A, Zone one, one moisture probe, one valve, shared pump, owned by Growlink, run by the head grower. A working Growlink probe may still be unable to connect to Home Assistant. The current operator keeps caring for the crop while you plan. Next, keep the old records safe.

visual.title: Moving house starts with a labelled inventory

check.prompt: You want to move Room A from Growlink to Crop Steering. What do you do first?

options.text: Record one zone’s equipment, settings and owner without changing anything
options.feedback: Right. A clear record of today’s setup is your starting point and your way back.

options.text: Switch Growlink off for the whole room
options.feedback: The plants would lose their water, and you lose the working baseline.

options.text: Plug the Growlink probes into Home Assistant
options.feedback: Compatibility is unknown. Check each probe’s documents first, as in C5.

slides.title: Keep the records in their original context
body: Use exports your account offers, or copy by hand
Keep original files, dates, units and timezone
The same label in two systems can mean different things
slides.narration: Photos of the old house help you set up the new one. Old records do the same job here. An export is a file a program saves so you can open the data somewhere else, such as a spreadsheet. Some products also offer an API, a doorway that lets other software fetch data automatically. Use only what your own Growlink account actually shows. If it offers neither, copy settings and history by hand or with screenshots. Keep the original files and their dates unchanged. Look at the cues on screen. Write down the timezone, lights-on and lights-off times, and substrate per plant. Add plant and dripper counts, measured flow, targets and how each value was measured. For example, a value labelled EC needs a note of where it was measured: tank, runoff or substrate. Crop Steering does not read Growlink files. You will enter checked values yourself on the Setup screen from lesson C four. Next, match old names to real equipment.

visual.title: Keep the records in their original context

check.prompt: An old Growlink record says EC 2.4, with no note of where it was measured. What do you write beside it?

options.text: Method unknown; find out before using it
options.feedback: Right. Feed, runoff and substrate EC are different measurements. Record the gap.

options.text: Pore-water EC
options.feedback: That is a guess. A wrong label could feed the Controller the wrong kind of EC.

options.text: Feed EC, because most records are
options.feedback: Still a guess. Check the original setup or ask the person who ran it.

slides.title: Example: one old zone, several new addresses
body: Old label: Room A, Zone 1
Same friendly name does not prove the same device
Write exact new entity IDs beside the old record
slides.narration: A contact called Mum on a new phone is only useful if the number is right. Names in two systems work the same way. Each Home Assistant entity has a friendly name, the readable label people see, such as Room A Zone one valve. It also has an entity ID, the exact address software uses, from lesson C three. Imagine Growlink calls a valve Room A, Zone one. Your Home Assistant now has an entity with that same friendly name. That match proves nothing about the real device. Someone may have typed the label onto the wrong valve. Look at the cues on screen. Trace the actual valve and probe with the installer. Confirm the interface, units and data age, as in lesson C five. Write the exact new entity ID beside the old record. Mark anything you cannot confirm as unknown. Then use lesson C four’s mapping and sizing checks to enter values. Old targets may mean something different in Crop Steering’s fields. Next, plan the handover.

visual.title: Example: one old zone, several new addresses

workedExample.prompt: Does a matching valve name prove the zone is ready to move?
steps: Keep the original Growlink room and zone record.
Trace the physical valve and write its exact new entity ID.
Confirm compatible control and one owner before commissioning.
workedExample.answer: No. A matching friendly name proves neither the real device nor who controls it.

check.prompt: switch.zone_1_valve has the friendly name Room A Zone 1. What proves it is the real Zone 1 valve?

options.text: Tracing it to the physical valve with the installer
options.feedback: Right. Only a physical trace links an entity to real equipment.

options.text: The friendly name matches the Growlink label
options.feedback: Anyone can type any label. A name is not a physical check.

options.text: It updated a minute ago
options.feedback: Fresh data shows communication, not which valve it controls.

slides.title: Agree the handover and the way back
body: Handover: the moment a zone changes controller
One controller per output, before and after
Rollback: checked steps back to the old setup
slides.narration: When a night nurse hands over to a day nurse, they agree the exact moment. Only one is in charge at a time. A handover is that moment for a zone, when control of its valve moves from Growlink to Crop Steering. Plan it with the responsible operator and the installer. Agree the time, which old controls get disabled, and how the plants get water during the work. Look at the diagram on screen. Each physical output has one controller at a time. Crop Steering may observe read-only, as in lesson C five, but it must never command a valve that Growlink still runs. Also write a rollback. A rollback is a checked set of steps to put the old arrangement back if a check fails. For example: make sure Crop Steering can no longer run Zone one, re-enable its Growlink schedule, then watch one shot start and stop. A rollback never means leaving both schedules running in case one fails. Next, try a review yourself.

visual.title: Agree the handover and the way back
visual.alt: Agree one output owner and a checked way back before the handover.

check.prompt: On handover day, Growlink’s Zone 1 schedule stays active as a backup while Crop Steering runs Zone 1. Is that safe?

options.text: No; disable one so the valve has a single owner
options.feedback: Right. Two owners can double-water or leave the valve open. Keep a rollback, not a second schedule.

options.text: Yes; a backup schedule is safer
options.feedback: A live second schedule is a competing controller. The rollback plan is your backup.

options.text: Yes, if their start times differ
options.feedback: Different times still mean extra shots. One output needs one owner.

slides.title: Your turn: the name matches, the method is unknown
body: Old EC method unknown; new field wants pore-water EC
Valve name matches, but nobody traced it
Park both mappings; keep the current checked owner
slides.narration: Now review a different record yourself. Pause after each fact and decide. Fact one: the old sensor is labelled EC, and nobody knows how it was measured. The Crop Steering field expects pore-water EC, the salts in the water between substrate pieces. Fact two: the valve’s friendly name matches, but no one has traced it to the real valve. Look at the cues on screen. Both gaps stay open. A familiar-looking screen cannot close them. So park both mappings. That means leave them out for now and list them as unresolved. Investigate the EC method, and trace the valve with the installer. Meanwhile the zone stays with its current, checked owner, here Growlink. Once both gaps are closed, finish the checks from lessons C three to C five. Then plan lesson C six’s two stages. A guess here could feed the Controller a wrong number or switch the wrong valve. Next, prove the zone.

visual.title: Your turn: the name matches, the method is unknown

check.prompt: Old record: EC 3.1, method unknown. Crop Steering’s field wants pore-water EC. What do you map?

options.text: Nothing yet; leave it unmapped and find out the method
options.feedback: Right. Park the mapping and investigate. Guessed EC misleads the Controller.

options.text: The old sensor, because 3.1 looks normal
options.feedback: A normal-looking number can still be the wrong kind of EC.

options.text: The feed tank EC entity instead
options.feedback: Feed EC is not pore-water EC. Swapping it in hides the gap.

slides.title: Prove one zone before expanding
body: At handover: shutdown, owner change, then C6 stages
Check fails: new output stays off, follow the rollback
Expand one zone at a time, repeating every check
slides.narration: A builder proves one room is watertight before plastering the next. Do the same with zones. At the agreed handover, follow the approved shutdown and ownership steps. Then run lesson C six’s commissioning on this zone. Remember the two stages: an installer-run equipment test with Watering OFF, then a supervised Controller cycle. Look at the cues on screen. Check acknowledged mapping, fresh readings, measured flow and water stopping. Check approved targets and light timing too. Supervise the first enabled cycle, and record its event and the final state. If any check fails, keep the new output off and follow your rollback. Expand only when this zone’s record is complete. For example, Zone one passes on Monday. Zone two still needs its own catch, stop and supervised cycle, even if it looks identical. Keep the old records and the rollback until every zone is proven. After the quiz, lesson D one opens the Overview screen you will use every day.

visual.title: Prove one zone before expanding
labels: Expand one zone at a time

check.prompt: Zone 1 passed every C6 check. Zone 2 uses the same valve model and dripper layout. What does Zone 2 need?

options.text: Its own handover, catch test, stop check and supervised cycle
options.feedback: Right. Each output is proven separately. Identical parts can be wired or plumbed differently.

options.text: Nothing; Zone 1 already proved the design
options.feedback: Zone 1’s record covers Zone 1 only. A crossed wire on Zone 2 would go unnoticed.

options.text: A catch test only
options.feedback: Catching water is one item. Mapping, stopping and the supervised cycle are needed too.

practice.prompt: Build a one-zone Growlink handover sheet: original records, physical labels, checked new entity IDs, one owner per output, crop-care cover, commissioning gates and rollback steps.
hints: Mark anything you cannot confirm as unknown, rather than guessing.
If you have no Growlink system, complete the sheet for the made-up Room A, Zone 1.
practice.success: The sheet keeps the original records, links each new entity ID to traced equipment, names one owner per output and lists checked rollback steps. Zone 1 is proven before any other zone moves.

quiz.prompt: What is the first useful step in a migration from Growlink?

options.text: Observe and record one existing zone and its owner
options.feedback: Right. Record today’s working setup before you change control.

options.text: Disable every existing schedule at once
options.feedback: That leaves plants without water and removes your baseline. Change one zone at a time.

options.text: Assume every Growlink probe connects to Home Assistant
options.feedback: Compatibility needs checking against each probe’s documents.

quiz.prompt: Old and new fields are both labelled EC. What must you check?

options.text: Measurement method, location and units
options.feedback: Right. Feed, runoff, bulk and pore-water EC are different measurements.

options.text: Only whether the numbers look similar
options.feedback: Similar numbers can come from different measurements.

options.text: Nothing; all EC fields are interchangeable
options.feedback: They are not. Feed EC is not pore-water EC, for example.

quiz.prompt: May Growlink and Crop Steering both command the same valve during migration?

options.text: No; one controller owns each physical output
options.feedback: Right. Crop Steering may observe read-only, but only one system sends commands.

options.text: Yes; their schedules sort out conflicts
options.feedback: Neither system knows the other exists. They can double-water or fight.

options.text: Yes, while the new dashboard is open
options.feedback: An open dashboard changes nothing. Ownership must be single.

quiz.prompt: One moved zone passed its supervised checks. What next?

options.text: Record its final state, then repeat every check for the next output
options.feedback: Right. Evidence for one output never commissions another.

options.text: Enable every other zone without testing
options.feedback: Untested zones can hide wrong wiring or plumbing. Prove each one.

options.text: Delete the old records and the rollback plan
options.feedback: Keep them until every zone is proven. They are your way back.

instructions: First build the handover sheet for the made-up Room A, Zone 1 on paper, or practise in the demo, which runs no equipment.
Build a one-zone Growlink handover sheet: original records, physical labels, checked new entity IDs, one owner per output, crop-care cover, commissioning gates and rollback steps.

For real equipment, work only with the responsible operator, the competent installer, the installation’s approved procedure and the agreed physical shutdown. Record what was checked and what is still unresolved.
